blocks.text: Bright Data in 2026: what you get

Bright Data, formerly Luminati, is the default enterprise pick for teams that want every collection tool under one contract. Its residential pool is one of the deepest available (150M+ advertised IPs across 195 countries), targeting goes down to city, ZIP and ASN, and the company layers managed products such as Web Unlocker and the Scraping Browser on top. You pay for that breadth: entry pricing is the highest of the major providers unless a promotion is running, and access to some target categories requires a compliance review.

Strengths: Deepest targeting in the market (ZIP, ASN, carrier); Managed unblocking, SERP and browser products under one account; Mature compliance and KYC processes that enterprise buyers ask for; Very large residential pool for high-rotation work. Weak spots: Highest list price per GB at low volume; Dashboard and zone setup take time to learn; Some targets need a compliance review before access.
Proxys.io in 2026: what you get

PROXYS.IO offers both rented static addresses and a rotating residential network. The provider reports more than 100 million ISP addresses across 195 countries, country/region/city targeting, up to 100 saved parameter sets and rotation every 2-60 minutes. Its mobile service covers 14 countries with city/carrier selection and roughly 2,000-5,000 addresses per country/carrier combination. Static IPv4 covers 24 markets. These are supplied specifications, not independently measured availability. HTTP, HTTPS and SOCKS5 are included on every plan.

Strengths: Low-entry per-address products; a provider-reported 100M+ residential network; country, region and city targeting; HTTP/HTTPS/SOCKS5 included; a 24-hour refund window. Weak spots: Rotating mobile traffic pricing must be checked in the cart; residential plans have 30/60/90-day validity; published pool totals do not guarantee reachable IPs; independent target-specific performance has not been established here.
Pricing: Bright Data vs Proxys.io

Bright Data lists residential traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, and it frequently runs 50%-off promotions that bring that to about $4/GB. Monthly plans start with the Growth tier at $499 for roughly 141 GB (about $3.50/GB) and fall to around $2.50/GB on the largest public plan.

PROXYS.IO separates traffic-based plans from per-address rentals. Rotating residential starts at $1.50/GB on 30, 60 or 90-day plans, without an IP or session cap. Static monthly starting prices are IPv6 $0.13, dynamic $0.27, shared IPv4 $0.67 (up to three users), foreign individual IPv4 $1.47, Windows-fingerprint IPv4 $1.87 and premium static residential IPv4 $3.60. Dedicated mobile IPv4 with unlimited traffic on a private channel starts at $56.79/month. Rotating mobile traffic is priced by the cart slider; no single starting per-GB rate has been confirmed. HEAT_RES provides 35% off eligible residential pay-per-traffic plans. Minimum static rental is one month and the refund window is 24 hours.

At 10 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because Proxys.io does not publish an exact price for that volume; Bright Data comes to about $80. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because Proxys.io does not publish an exact price for that volume; Bright Data comes to about $499. Both Bright Data and Proxys.io work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

PROXYS.IO reports a residential pool of 100M+ ISP addresses; this has not been independently audited. Bright Data lists '150M+' and Proxys.io reports 100M+ addresses. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, Bright Data lists 195 countries and Proxys.io lists 195 residential countries, with separate mobile and static coverage. On targeting, Bright Data offers country, state, city, ZIP, ASN and carrier, while Proxys.io offers country, region and city for residential traffic, with city/carrier selection for mobile.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Bright Data offers rotating per request or sticky sessions you control per zone, and Proxys.io offers static per-IP proxies; rotating residential and mobile. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?
General web scraping: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: its pool depth and Web Unlocker handle hardened targets. How Proxys.io compares: it is a per-IP shop, not a large rotating pool.
SERP and rank tracking: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: it sells a dedicated SERP API alongside raw proxies. How Proxys.io compares: cheap IPv6 can handle some search tasks.

Social media and multi-account management: Proxys.io. Proxys.io has the edge here. Why: fixed dedicated or mobile IPs per account. How Bright Data compares: it is powerful but expensive for low-volume account work.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: ZIP-level targeting suits local pricing and stock checks. How Proxys.io compares: limited rotation for large catalog crawls.

Ad verification and geo-testing: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: carrier and ASN targeting reproduce what real users see. The limitation on the Proxys.io side: limited geo depth.
Tight budgets: Proxys.io. Proxys.io has the edge here. Why: cheap per-IP rentals with unlimited bandwidth. How Bright Data compares: its list price is the highest in this comparison.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Bright Data: Free trial for business accounts, no card required. Proxys.io: 24-hour refund window instead of a trial. Verification and payment rules differ too. Bright Data: Verification required for some sensitive targets. Proxys.io: Light; crypto accepted. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Bright Data and Proxys.io before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Bright Data vs Proxys.io faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Bright Data: free trial for business accounts, no card required; Proxys.io: 24-hour refund window instead of a trial).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.

3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country. 4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Bright Data comes out ahead in 4, Proxys.io in 2, and 0 are ties. That makes Bright Data the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Bright Data is strongest for enterprise data teams with budget for managed tooling, while Proxys.io is strongest for multi-account and affiliate work that needs fixed IPs. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
